title: Amino acids
outcomes: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
Essential, uncommon and modified amino acids

summary.overview: Proteins are built from 20 L-α-amino acids. All share an amino group, a carboxyl group and an H on the α-carbon, and differ only in their R group. The R group decides polarity, charge, reactivity and light absorption, and ionisation sets each amino acid's charge at a given pH.

sections.heading: Structure and stereochemistry
points: The α-carbon carries –COOH, –NH2, –H and an R group. In every amino acid except glycine (R = H) it is a chiral centre.
Proline is an imino acid: its side chain loops back onto the α-nitrogen (a secondary amine), forming a rigid ring.

D/L describes absolute configuration relative to D/L-glyceraldehyde (Fischer). d/l, or (+)/(−), describes the direction of optical rotation. R/S describes each individual stereocentre. These three systems are not equivalent.
Proteins contain only L-amino acids, because ribosomes are stereospecific; D-amino acids occur in bacterial cell walls.
Chirality matters for drugs: thalidomide's S-enantiomer is teratogenic, and the two enantiomers interconvert in the body. Only S(−)-amlodipine blocks calcium channels.

sections.heading: Five classes by R group
points: Non-polar aliphatic (7): Gly, Ala, Pro, Val, Leu, Ile, Met. These cluster in the protein interior (hydrophobic effect).
Aromatic (3): Phe, Tyr, Trp. They absorb UV at about 280 nm, Trp most strongly, so protein concentration can be found with A = εcl.
Polar uncharged (5): Ser, Thr, Cys, Asn, Gln. These form H-bonds; two Cys can oxidise to cystine, forming a disulfide bond.
Positively charged (3): Lys and Arg are fully protonated at pH 7; His (pKa ≈ 6) can be neutral or positive, which makes it a buffer and a catalyst.
Negatively charged (2): aspartate and glutamate, which carry a –COO⁻ at physiological pH.

sections.heading: Ionisation and pI
points: Each amino acid has at least two ionisable groups: α-COOH (pKa ≈ 2) and α-NH3⁺ (pKa ≈ 9–10).
At low pH the amino acid is a cation; at high pH an anion; in between it is a zwitterion with both + and − charges (amphoteric).
The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which the net charge is zero. For an amino acid without an ionisable side chain, pI = (pK1 + pK2)/2; for glycine, (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97.
Below its pI a molecule is net positive; above its pI it is net negative. This is the basis of ion-exchange chromatography and isoelectric focusing.

sections.heading: Essential, uncommon and modified amino acids
points: Essential amino acids cannot be made in sufficient amounts and must come from the diet. Requirements differ between species; cats, for example, need dietary arginine.
Selenocysteine is the only uncommon amino acid inserted by the ribosome.

Others arise by post-translational modification: 4-hydroxyproline in collagen (needs vitamin C), γ-carboxyglutamate in clotting factors (needs vitamin K), and reversible phosphorylation of Ser, Thr and Tyr.
Free methionine is an important methyl donor in metabolism (as S-adenosylmethionine).

keyTerms.definition: Central carbon bearing the amino, carboxyl, H and R groups.
Molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge, with no net charge.
pH at which a molecule has zero net charge.
Able to act as both an acid and a base.
Proline, whose α-nitrogen is a secondary amine within a ring.
Two cysteines joined by a disulfide (S–S) bond.
Amino acid that must be supplied in the diet.

examTips: Glycine is the only standard amino acid that is NOT chiral.
L/D is NOT the same as the direction of optical rotation (+/−).
pH < pI → net positive; pH > pI → net negative.
Lys and Arg are positive and Asp and Glu negative at pH 7; His is the borderline one (pKa ≈ 6).

questions.outcome: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
questions.stem: Why is glycine the only standard amino acid that is not chiral?

options.text: Its R group is a hydrogen atom, so its α-carbon carries two identical groups
options.why: A chiral centre needs four different groups; glycine has two H atoms on the α-carbon.

options.text: It has no carboxyl group, so its α-carbon carries only three different groups
options.why: Glycine has both α-carboxyl and α-amino groups.

options.text: Its α-carbon forms a rigid ring with the amino nitrogen, so it cannot be chiral
options.why: That describes proline, which is chiral.

options.text: It occurs only as the D-isomer in nature, so there is no mirror-image form of it
options.why: Without a chiral centre glycine has no D/L forms.

questions.outcome: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
questions.stem: What does the 'L' in L-alanine refer to?

options.text: Its absolute configuration, by comparison with L-glyceraldehyde in a Fischer projection
options.why: D/L is a configurational label based on glyceraldehyde, not a measured optical property.

options.text: That it rotates plane-polarised light to the left, as measured with a polarimeter
options.why: Left rotation is denoted l or (−); some L-amino acids are dextrorotatory.

options.text: The R/S configuration of each stereocentre in the molecule, assigned by priority rules
options.why: R/S is a separate system based on priority rules for each centre.

options.text: That it is a large (long-chain) amino acid with more than three carbons in its side chain
options.why: L has nothing to do with size.

questions.outcome: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
questions.stem: Thalidomide's R-enantiomer is the therapeutic form and the S-enantiomer is teratogenic. Why would giving pure R-thalidomide not have prevented birth defects?

options.text: The two enantiomers interconvert (racemise) in the body, so some S-form forms anyway
options.why: Thalidomide racemises in vivo, so a single-enantiomer formulation does not stay single.

options.text: Enantiomers always have identical biological effects, so the R-form is teratogenic too
options.why: Chiral receptors often distinguish enantiomers, as amlodipine shows.

options.text: R-thalidomide is a diastereomer of the S-form, and diastereomers are equally harmful
options.why: Mirror-image R and S forms of one centre are enantiomers.

options.text: Ribosomes convert R-drugs into S-drugs when they are absorbed in the small intestine
options.why: Ribosomes synthesise proteins; they don't convert drugs.

questions.outcome: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
questions.stem: Why does proline often interrupt α-helices in globular proteins?

options.text: Its side chain is fused to the α-nitrogen in a rigid ring, and that nitrogen has no H to donate
options.why: Proline is an imino acid; its constrained geometry introduces kinks.

options.text: It carries a large negative charge that repels the partial negative end of the helix dipole
options.why: Proline's side chain is non-polar and uncharged.

options.text: It forms disulfide bonds with nearby residues, which pull the polypeptide out of the helix
options.why: Only cysteine forms disulfide bonds.

options.text: It is a D-amino acid, so its side chain points the wrong way for a right-handed α-helix
options.why: Proline in proteins is the L-isomer.

questions.stem: Which amino acids carry a full positive charge on their side chain at pH 7?

options.text: Lysine and arginine
options.why: Their side-chain pKa values (≈ 10.5 and 12.5) are well above 7, so they stay protonated.

options.text: Aspartate and glutamate
options.why: These are negatively charged (carboxylates) at pH 7.

options.text: Serine and threonine
options.why: These are polar but uncharged.

options.text: Phenylalanine and tryptophan
options.why: These are aromatic and uncharged.

questions.stem: In a water-soluble globular protein, where would you mainly expect to find Leu, Val and Ile residues, and why?

options.text: Buried in the interior, because burying non-polar side chains is favoured by the hydrophobic effect
options.why: The hydrophobic effect is the main driving force for folding globular proteins.

options.text: On the surface, where their side chains form hydrogen bonds with the surrounding water molecules
options.why: Their aliphatic side chains can't form H-bonds.

options.text: On the surface, forming salt bridges with Lys side chains that stabilise the folded protein
options.why: Salt bridges need charged side chains.

options.text: Only in disulfide bonds, where their side chains link two strands of the polypeptide
options.why: Disulfides involve only cysteine.

questions.stem: A protein has a molar absorption coefficient at 280 nm of 25 000 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹. In a 1 cm cuvette its A280 is 0.50. What is its concentration?

options.text: 20 µM
options.why: Beer–Lambert: c = A/(εl) = 0.50 / 25 000 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ M = 20 µM.
This multiplies A by ε instead of dividing.

options.text: 2 µM
options.why: This is out by a factor of 10; 0.5/25 000 = 0.00002 M.

options.text: 50 mM
options.why: Concentration must be A divided by εl.

questions.stem: Which amino acid side chains are mainly responsible for proteins absorbing UV light at about 280 nm?

options.text: Tryptophan and tyrosine (aromatic)
options.why: They are the strongest chromophores, Trp most of all; Phe absorbs weakly.

options.text: Lysine and arginine (basic)
options.why: Basic side chains do not absorb significantly at 280 nm.

options.text: Glycine and alanine (small)
options.why: Small aliphatic side chains don't absorb at 280 nm.

options.text: Aspartate and glutamate (acidic)
options.why: Carboxylates don't absorb at 280 nm.

questions.stem: Free histidine is mostly uncharged at pH 7.4, but histidine side chains in proteins often act as buffers and catalysts. Why?

options.text: Its imidazole pKa (≈ 6) is close to physiological pH, so it can easily be protonated or neutral
options.why: Small shifts in the local environment can switch His between charged and uncharged forms.

options.text: Its side chain is negatively charged at pH 7, so it can bind any proton that is released
options.why: His is weakly basic; it can be neutral or positive.

options.text: It forms disulfide bonds with substrates, holding them in the active site during catalysis
options.why: Only Cys forms disulfides.

options.text: Its side-chain pKa is about 12, like arginine, so it stays protonated across the cell's pH range
options.why: Arg's pKa is about 12.5; His's is about 6.

questions.stem: Glycine has pK1 (α-COOH) = 2.34 and pK2 (α-NH3⁺) = 9.60. What is its isoelectric point?

options.why: With no ionisable side chain, pI = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97.
This is the sum of the pKa values, not their average.
pI is not automatically neutral pH.
This is half of pK2 minus pK1, not the average of the two.

questions.stem: What is the predominant form of alanine at pH 7?

options.text: A zwitterion, ⁺H3N–CH(CH3)–COO⁻, with no net charge
options.why: pH 7 lies between the two pKa values (≈ 2.3 and ≈ 9.7), so the carboxyl is deprotonated and the amino group protonated.

options.text: H2N–CH(CH3)–COOH, the neutral form with no charges at all
options.why: This form is negligible in water at any pH.

options.text: The fully protonated cation, ⁺H3N–CH(CH3)–COOH
options.why: This dominates only below pH ≈ 2.

options.text: The fully deprotonated anion, H2N–CH(CH3)–COO⁻
options.why: This dominates only above pH ≈ 10.

questions.stem: A protein with pI = 5.0 is placed in a buffer at pH 7.5. What is its net charge, and towards which electrode will it move in an electric field?

options.text: Net negative; it moves towards the anode (+)
options.why: Above its pI a protein loses protons and carries a net negative charge.

options.text: Net positive; it moves towards the cathode (−)
options.why: A protein is net positive only below its pI.

options.text: Zero; it does not move
options.why: Zero net charge occurs only at pH = pI.

options.text: Net negative; it moves towards the cathode (−)
options.why: Negative molecules move towards the positive electrode.

questions.outcome: Essential, uncommon and modified amino acids
questions.stem: A cat fed a single arginine-free meal can develop vomiting and neurological signs within hours. What is the biochemical explanation?

options.text: Cats can't make enough arginine, so the urea cycle can't dispose of ammonia: hyperammonaemia
options.why: Arginine is a urea-cycle intermediate; cats rely on dietary arginine, so a deficiency quickly causes ammonia toxicity.

options.text: Arginine is the only source of glucose in cats, so without it they quickly become hypoglycaemic
options.why: Many amino acids and glycerol are gluconeogenic.

options.text: Arginine is needed to make the D-amino acids in feline proteins, so new proteins cannot fold
options.why: Proteins contain only L-amino acids.

options.text: Without arginine, cats cannot absorb water from the gut, so they become dehydrated within hours
options.why: The problem is ammonia detoxification.

questions.outcome: Essential, uncommon and modified amino acids
questions.stem: Which uncommon amino acid is inserted directly by the ribosome during translation rather than formed by post-translational modification?

options.text: Selenocysteine
options.why: Selenocysteine has its own tRNA and is inserted at a recoded UGA codon.

options.text: 4-Hydroxyproline
options.why: It is made after translation by prolyl hydroxylase, which needs vitamin C.

options.text: γ-Carboxyglutamate
options.why: It is formed after translation by a vitamin K-dependent carboxylase.

options.text: Phosphoserine
options.why: It is formed by kinases after translation.

questions.stem: What happens when two cysteine side chains in a protein are oxidised?

options.text: They form a covalent disulfide bond (a cystine residue) that stabilises the structure
options.why: The –SH groups oxidise to –S–S–, an important covalent cross-link.

options.text: They form a peptide bond between their side chains, linking two parts of the chain
options.why: Peptide bonds link α-carboxyl and α-amino groups.

options.text: They become positively charged and repel each other, unfolding that part of the protein
options.why: Disulfide formation doesn't add positive charge.

options.text: They are converted into methionine residues by adding a methyl group to each sulfur
options.why: Oxidation joins two Cys; it doesn't make Met.

flashcards.outcome: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
flashcards.back: Carboxyl, amino, hydrogen and the R group (in glycine, R = H, so it is not chiral).

flashcards.outcome: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
flashcards.back: D/L: configuration relative to glyceraldehyde. d/l (+/−): direction of optical rotation. R/S: configuration of each individual stereocentre.

flashcards.outcome: Structure and stereochemistry of amino acids
flashcards.front: Which isomers are found in proteins?
flashcards.back: Only L-amino acids (ribosomes are stereospecific). D-amino acids occur in bacterial cell walls.
Non-polar aliphatic (7), aromatic (3), polar uncharged (5), positively charged (3), negatively charged (2).
+: Lys, Arg (and His, partly). −: Asp, Glu.

flashcards.front: Why do proteins absorb at 280 nm?
flashcards.back: Aromatic side chains, mainly Trp and Tyr. Concentration from A = εcl.
A form with both +NH3 and −COO⁻ and no net charge. It dominates between the two pKa values.

flashcards.front: pI of a simple amino acid?

flashcards.back: pH < pI → net positive. pH = pI → zero. pH > pI → net negative.

flashcards.outcome: Essential, uncommon and modified amino acids
flashcards.front: Examples of modified amino acids, and their vitamins?
flashcards.back: 4-Hydroxyproline (collagen, vitamin C); γ-carboxyglutamate (clotting factors, vitamin K); phospho-Ser/Thr/Tyr (signalling). Selenocysteine is inserted by the ribosome.
